lines.text: Take [[f|$f(t) = t^2$]] again, and shade the area up to a moving edge, $x$.
lines.say: Take t squared again, and shade the area up to a moving edge, x.

lines.text: Call that area [[a|$A(x)$]]. Slide the edge right, and $A(x)$ traces its own curve.
lines.say: Call that area, Eigh of x. Slide the edge right, and Eigh of x traces its own curve.

lines.text: The question that ties it all together: [[d|how fast does the area grow]]?
lines.say: Here's the question that ties it all together: how fast does the area grow?

lines.text: Nudge the edge right by a tiny $dx$. The area gains a thin [[d|sliver]].
lines.say: Nudge the edge right, by a tiny d x. The area gains a thin sliver.

lines.text: The sliver is nearly a rectangle: height $f(x)$, width $dx$. So $dA \approx f(x)\,dx$.
lines.say: The sliver is nearly a rectangle: height f of x, width d x.

lines.text: Divide by $dx$ and let it shrink: $\frac{dA}{dx} = f(x)$.
lines.say: Divide by d x, and let it shrink: d Eigh by d x is f of x.

lines.text: Check: the slope of $A$ at $x = 1.4$ is 1.96, exactly $f(1.4)$.
lines.say: Check: the slope here is one point nine six.

lines.text: That is the [[w|fundamental theorem]]: the derivative of the accumulated area is the original function.
lines.say: That's the fundamental theorem: the derivative of the area is the original function.

lines.text: Turned around: to find an area, find any $F$ whose derivative is $f$…
lines.say: Turned around: to find an area, find any F whose derivative is f,

lines.text: …and subtract its values at the two ends. No rectangles required.
lines.say: and subtract its values at the two ends. No rectangles required.

lines.text: Back to chapter 2: $t^3/3$ has derivative $t^2$, so the area is $F(2) - F(0)$.
lines.say: Back to chapter two. t cubed over three has derivative t squared.

lines.text: Exactly $\tfrac{8}{3}$: the number 256 rectangles were creeping toward, now in one line.
lines.say: Exactly eight thirds: the number our rectangles crept toward, now in one line.
Derivatives measure change. Integrals add it up. Each one undoes the other.
